opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that "one shot" runs into a few different walls at once.

The first is that a clinical candidate isn't optimized for one thing, it's a balancing act across dozens of properties simultaneously. You need potency against your target, but also selectivity against related proteins, solubility, permeability, metabolic stability, low hERG liability, no reactive metabolites, reasonable half-life, oral bioavailability if that's what you want, and it has to be synthesizable at scale. Generative models are getting quite good at satisfying a handful of those constraints, especially the ones we can compute or predict reliably, like binding pose or basic physicochemical properties. But many of the properties that actually kill molecules in development, things like in vivo PK, off-target toxicity, idiosyncratic liver tox, are exactly the ones where our predictive models are weakest.

That ties into the second barrier, which is data. For binding we have structures, we have physics, we have a lot of assay data. For ADMET and especially for in vivo outcomes, the public data is thin, noisy, and inconsistent across labs. A lot of the really valuable data sits inside pharma companies and was generated under different protocols over decades. So the model can only be as good as its oracle, and for the hardest endpoints the oracle is pretty fuzzy.

Third, there's the biology itself. Even a molecule that's perfect on paper is a bet on a hypothesis: that hitting this target in this patient population will actually change the disease. No amount of chemistry optimization fixes a wrong target. Most clinical failures are really efficacy failures, and that's a biology problem, not a generation problem.

And then practically, medicinal chemistry is inherently iterative. The design-make-test-analyze loop exists because every round teaches you something you couldn't have predicted, like an unexpected metabolite or a solubility cliff. So I think the more realistic near-term goal isn't true one-shot generation, it's dramatically compressing that loop: fewer cycles, smarter experiments, models that learn from each round in active-learning fashion. If you can go from, say, synthesizing a few thousand compounds to a few hundred to reach a candidate, that's an enormous win, even if it's not literally one shot.

So I'm optimistic, but I think the bottleneck is shifting from "can we generate good-looking molecules," which we largely can now, to "can we predict and measure the things that actually matter in a human body."

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest barrier is that generating a molecule and knowing that it’s going to work as a drug are very different problems. You can propose something that looks plausible, or even something that binds very strongly to a target. But that’s only one of the properties you need.

It also has to get to the right tissue, stay around long enough, avoid interacting with other targets in harmful ways, and be something you can actually manufacture. Those constraints interact. You change a molecule to improve one property, and you may make another property worse.

Then there’s the biological question: even if you hit the target exactly as intended, does that actually help the patient? A molecule-generation model doesn’t automatically resolve that uncertainty.

So to get to something almost clinic-ready in one shot, you’d need to predict a whole chain of experimental outcomes reliably. And the data you’d want for that are sparse, uneven, and often missing the failures. I think the more practical path is a tight loop between models and experiments: propose molecules, test them, and use what you learn to make the next round better. Getting that loop to converge much faster would already be a huge advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest barrier is that we don’t have a complete way to tell whether a molecule is going to make a good drug. You can generate something that looks plausible, or even something that binds really well to a target, but that’s only one part of the problem. Does it get to the right tissue? Does it stay around long enough? Is it toxic? Can you manufacture it? Those constraints all have to work together.

And the data we have is pretty sparse and biased toward the things people have chosen to test. For any given molecule, you usually don’t have measurements across all of those dimensions. So a model can get very good at optimizing the properties you can measure and still miss something that matters in a person.

I’d expect progress to come from tighter loops between generation and experiments. You propose molecules, test them, and use those results to improve the next round. Getting something almost ready for the clinic in one shot would require a much better ability to predict human biology than we have today.
